analysis.one_liner: Bans the manufacture, use, and sale of commercial asbestos, with a multi-year phase-out for chemical plants.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the Senate on August 4, 2026 and referred to the Environment and Public Works Committee, where it sits with no further action; one Republican senator cosponsored it.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the Toxic Substances Control Act to ban the manufacture, processing, use, and sale of commercial asbestos — the material that causes mesothelioma and other cancers. It takes effect immediately on enactment, but carves out exceptions: chlor-alkali plants (which make chlorine and lye and are the last US industry importing raw asbestos) could keep using asbestos until 2032, or 2036 for companies that had multiple facilities using it in 2024; asbestos sheet gaskets get a phase-out set by the EPA; the President can grant up to six years of national-security exemptions; and asbestos already installed in buildings is left alone. The bill was introduced with one Republican cosponsor and referred to committee, where it has sat with no further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and the public: anyone who might breathe asbestos fibers from imported products, chemical-plant workers near chlor-alkali facilities, and families affected by mesothelioma and other asbestos cancers. The US already banned new asbestos products decades ago, but imports of asbestos-containing items and industrial use continued.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and anyone exposed to asbestos products

how_it_helps.text: It immediately prohibits any manufacture, processing, use, or sale of commercial asbestos in any of its eight defined forms, closing the door on a known carcinogen in new products.

It overrides the parts of the 2024 EPA rule that could have allowed longer timelines, putting a statutory end date on the two remaining legal uses (chlor-alkali diaphragms and sheet gaskets) instead of leaving them to agency discretion.
It requires public reporting of any national-security exemption the President grants, with only narrow classified exceptions.

analysis.who_pays: Chlor-alkali chemical plants that still use asbestos diaphragms must convert to alternative technology by 2032-2036, and businesses selling asbestos-containing products (gaskets, brakes, certain imported goods) lose that product line; some compliance costs may show up in prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Chlor-alkali plants and asbestos product sellers

drawbacks.text: The bill lets chlor-alkali plants keep using asbestos diaphragms until 2032, and until 2036 for companies that had more than one facility using asbestos in 2024, so the cancer-causing material stays in use for years after enactment.
The President may grant national-security exemptions from the ban, extendable to six years, and can withhold publication of those exemptions as classified, limiting public oversight.
Asbestos already installed in buildings and equipment stays in place; the ban covers new commercial distribution, not removal of existing asbestos.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health benefit of finally banning commercial asbestos is substantial and the compliance cost falls mostly on one or two companies that already face an EPA rule requiring a phase-out, so the trade-off favors the ban. The honest caveat is that the bill is slower than a full ban: up to six more years for some chlor-alkali plants and continued asbestos use in the meantime, plus a presidential national-security exemption that could stretch use up to six more years in undisclosed cases.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, and nothing has happened since, so it never came to a vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on August 4, 2026 and read twice, then referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, its only action so far.
No committee action, floor vote, or further movement is recorded; the Congress is still in session, so the bill is technically alive but stalled.
It has a single cosponsor, Senator Curtis (R-UT), whose office says she worked with Merkley on the bill, giving it one vote of the 55 Senate Republicans as backing beyond its Democratic sponsor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Chlor-alkali plants that use asbestos and other businesses selling asbestos-containing products keep operating under the current slower EPA phase-out, while workers and the public keep bearing exposure risk. Merkley's office has pushed similar bans across multiple congresses without success.

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its sole Democratic sponsor.

for.name: Sen. John Curtis
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, its only Republican support.

for.name: Asbestos-disease advocacy organizations (including the Asbestos Disease Awareness Organization)
for.what_they_did: Longtime backers of a version of this ban named for Alan Reinstein, a mesothelioma victim; they have pushed versions of the bill across several congresses.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's support is almost entirely from Democrats: one Democratic sponsor and a single Republican cosponsor out of 55, with no floor action to show how the rest of the Senate would vote.

industries.industry: Chlor-alkali chemical producers using asbestos diaphragms
industries.note: These are the only US plants still importing raw chrysotile asbestos; the bill gives them until 2032 (2036 for some) to finish converting to non-asbestos membrane technology, with interim exposure controls in the meantime. The cost of conversion is real but borne by a small number of large companies.

industries.industry: Asbestos importers, distributors, and sheet-gasket makers
industries.note: The ban immediately ends new commerce in asbestos-containing products except for a phased-out sheet-gasket pathway run under existing EPA rules. Ordinary consumers gain safer products, at some cost to any niche suppliers.

industries.industry: Asbestos abatement, disposal, and remediation contractors
industries.note: Because asbestos already installed stays in place, professional removal and disposal remains necessary for decades; the bill preserves that work while prohibiting new use.

analysis.trajectory: With a Republican Senate majority and only one Republican cosponsor, the bill is unlikely to get a committee markup or floor vote before the Congress ends on January 3, 2027, unless it is reintroduced in the next Congress.
